newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac, Kohl reaffirm euro confidence.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Kohl reaffirm euro confidence.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl have renewed their determination to launch a single European currency on time in 1999, French and German officials said on Thursday.
"They emphasised their total determination to launch the euro at the scheduled date," a French official said, reporting on talks in Bonn on Wednesday.

Bonn government spokesman Peter Hausmann said that, in addition to their ritual joint message of confidence in monetary union, the leaders agreed to work closely together to prepare a European Union summit on institutional reform in June on which there have been Franco-German differences.
Despite lingering doubts about Germany's ability to meet the fitness test for monetary union, Kohl's decision to stand for re-election next year has bolstered faith in the project.

Kohl and Chirac, who met in Bonn on Wednesday evening for informal talks, agreed to get together several more times ahead of a June summit in Amsterdam on the reform of EU institutions, the French official said.

Despite the two countries' leading role in pushing for the creation of a single currency, Paris and Bonn will have to overcome differences on EU reform to prevent its institutions becoming unwieldy as the 15-nation bloc expands membership.

France has pushed hard to reduce the executive European Commission to about 10 members -- fewer than the number of member states, meaning that each country would not be guaranteed a commissioner at all times.
The French have also sought ways of giving the bigger states more votes in the EU's weighted voting system in line with their population and economic power, diplomats said.
Germany wants to avoid the wrath of smaller member states which could lose out from such moves.

Diplomats said Paris and Bonn were closer together on the issues of European Commission reform and weighted voting than their public positions suggested at an EU foreign ministers' meeting in Noordwijk earlier this week.

They said the Germans sympathised with the French ideas but believed consensus could only be achieved by letting each member state nominate one commissioner -- whereas the five bigger states currently appoint two each.
There might then be some rotation between senior and junior commission posts.

On weighted voting, Bonn preferred a rule change stipulating that in any decision taken by qualified majority voting, the majority would also have to represent more than half of the EU's total population, the diplomats said.

This should prevent situations arising in which a coalition of small countries, which have more votes than is justified by their population, could impose their will on the bigger member states, which are the main budget contributors, they said.

It would also be a painlesss way of giving Germany -- the EU's most populous state, but which has the same number of votes as Britain, France and Italy -- a little extra weight without giving it more votes than its peers, the diplomats explained.
